senses: A monetary pool, in which tips are collected and later shared out between all staff, e.g. in a restaurant.
ety: Borrowed from French tronc des pauvres (“poor box”).

senses: Having limbs.
Preceded by a descriptive word: having limbs of a specified kind or quality.
ety: From Middle English ilimed (“having limbs, limbed”) [and other forms], from i- (prefix forming adjectives, past participles, etc.) + lim (“organ or part of the body, member; extremity of an animal or human body, limb; sexual organ; a person as a member of the group of all Christians; follower; liegeman; corner of a siege tower; arm of the sea; branch of a subject”) (see further at lim) + -ed (suffix forming adjectives); analysable as limb + -ed.

senses: A teacher of Hindu mysticism.
ety: From Sanskrit महर्षि (maharṣi, “great seer”) from महा (mahā, “great”) + ऋषि (ṛṣi, “saint, seer”).
examples: His lineage of teachers and masters included several famous maharishis.

senses: Meat or poultry cut into small pieces, stewed or fried and served in its own gravy.
ety: From French fricassée (noun), from fricassée, past participle of fricasser (verb).

senses: To tax to an excessive degree.
To overburden.
One who tolls a bell.
A machine for straightening and cleaning wool.
A yoga pose in which the practitioner lies prone with the torso erect, supported by the arms, and the head tilted back.
examples: Mary Dunn recommends moving into a variation of Updog that teaches you what is necessary to avoid compressing the lower back in the pose.
Push your shoulders back and lift the raised leg high, then drop back into the updog.
I don't think I'll ever forget watching one of my clients do a full expression of updog one week before giving birth. I was in awe at her grace.

senses: To remove (a yarn, fabric, equipment, etc.) from one's collection.
examples: She destashed some needles that I ended up taking off her hands last summer.

senses: Having or wearing a helmet, or having the appearance of wearing a helmet.
One of the three gunas in Hindu philosophy, representing things that are active, excitable, or passionate.
ety: From Sanskrit रजस् (rajas). Doublet of Erebus.

senses: The action of gasifying.
Pearl millet (Cenchrus americanus, syn. Pennisetum glaucum).
ety: From Hindi बाजरा (bājrā). Compare bajri from Gujarati બાજરી (bājrī).
examples: When food was scarce, the children would subsist on a lump of jaggery and one bajra roti each.

senses: Any fly of the family Phoridae.
To supply with new personnel.
A bus driver.
The quality of being an academic discipline.
The quality of being amenable to division into such disciplines.
The matching of a perceived attribute between objects with differing physical attributes.
A turning, twisting or spinning motion.
ety: Alteration of *twissel (“to double”), from twissel (“double, twofold”). More at twissel.

senses: A proposed unified currency of Canada, the United States, and Mexico.
ety: From America, perhaps modelled on euro; coined by Canadian politician Herb Grubel in 1999.
examples: From the US point of view, the key benefit of the amero model - reduced transactions costs - would be fully duplicated by the dollarization alternative.
The Amero would increase the GDP of the US by only roughly 15%.

senses: An open-topped sports car; a roadster.
ety: For the resemblance of the carriages' long, thin spokes to a spider's legs; the name was extended by analogy to open-topped automobiles.

senses: A thong of soft leather to bind up a hawk's wing.
A stock at each end of a seine to keep it stretched.
A rope or line used to suspend lights or scenery in a certain position.
The feathers around a hawk's rump.
ety: From Middle English brayle, from Old French braiel, from Medieval Latin bracale (“girdle”) (from bracae (“breeches”)).

senses: The lineage or clan assigned to a Hindu at birth.
That mesh between one another.
A hot iron for searing or cauterizing.
ety: From French cautère, Latin cauterium, from Ancient Greek καυτήρ (kautḗr), variant of καυστήρ (kaustḗr, “cauterizing apparatus”), from καίω (kaíō, “burn”)). Compare caustic, cautery.
examples: The punctuall, or pointed cauter; is almost square, and altogether Sharpe pointed

senses: A leg of lamb or mutton.
ety: Borrowed from French gigot (“leg (of lamb)”), from gigue (“(colloquial) a long leg; haunch of some animals, especially venison”) + -ot (diminutive suffix). Gigue is derived from giguer (“to dance; to jump”), further etymology unknown.

senses: Self-indulgent and ultimately unproductive; serving primarily to gratify oneself rather than producing anything meaningful or substantive.
A severe punishment prescribed for certain offenses, interpreted variously as expulsion or extinction of the soul.
A person who catches crabs.
ety: From crab (“crustacean having five pairs of legs”) + -er (occupational suffix) or + -er (relational noun suffix).
examples: Many shrimpers complain that the crabbers place their traps too close together and that they can't go between the traps without snagging their nets.

senses: A native or inhabitant of an isthmus.
A person who is transferred.
The state or condition of being viral: tendency to spread by word of mouth or memetic action.
examples: The point is virality—content so outlandish that people can’t help but talk about it.
Behind each seemingly off-the-cuff post (“DUDE LMAO THIS IS A GAS STATION😭😭😭”) were careful choices about how to compose the shot for maximum virality.

senses: That cannot be proved or verified by any test.
ety: From Middle English unprevable, wnprowabil, equivalent to un- + provable and to un- + prove + -able.

senses: sparkling; brilliant
ety: From mica + -aceous. From Latin mīca (“grain, crumb”). Often erroneously associated with Latin micō (“to twinkle, glitter”) and hence with English micacious.
examples: The book review was a micaceous example of perfection.

senses: A French alcoholic liqueur flavored with anise
ety: Borrowed from French anisette, from anis + -ette.

senses: A megaphone or bullhorn.
examples: It's a grotesque, misleading smear on a diverse group of individuals – a bit like claiming all Muslims are terrorists (which, coincidentally, the guy beside them is currently doing through a loudhailer).

senses: The science of authenticating, dating, and interpreting old official documents.
ety: Probably from Italian or Ecclesiastical Latin diplomatica.

senses: Any similar layer of an exoplanet.
A small, light, and usually savory first course in a meal.
Something that creates or increases excitement for what is to follow.
A Mediterranean tree (Pistacia terebinthus and, possibly, Pistacia palaestina)
ety: From Middle English therebynte, from Old French terebinthe, from Latin terebinthus, from Ancient Greek τερέβινθος (terébinthos), from Pre-Greek. Related to turpentine and terpene.
